extracted.intended_audience: medical researchers, science communicators, university press officers, and health journalists
extracted.subtask_description: A content-analysis coding scheme for comparing academic press releases and associated news against their peer-reviewed journal articles, focused on exaggeration in advice, causal claims, and inference to humans. Includes operational definitions, multi-level coding scales, sampling/inclusion rules, and metrics of news uptake and coding reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational definition of exaggeration
rubrics_metrics.description: Exaggeration is identified where news stories offered advice to readers, made causal claims, or inferred relevance to humans beyond (or different to) those stated in the associated peer reviewed journal article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a study reporting a correlation between stress and wine consumption and the news claiming 'wine causes stress'; a news claim of a treatment for humans when the study was on rodents. The journal article is taken as the baseline for comparison (with caveats that journal articles themselves may contain exaggeration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice coding (four levels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maximum level of advice in the text is coded using four levels based on explicitness and directness: (1) no advice, (2) implicit advice (e.g. 'these findings suggest that mid-late childhood may be the best bet for childhood obesity prevention'), (3) explicit advice but not to the reader or general public (e.g. 'pulse oximetry screening should be incorporated into everyday clinical practice'), and (4) explicit advice to the reader or general public (e.g. 'children who are thirsty should be encouraged to drink water').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each journal article, press release, and news story was coded for the maximum level of advice anywhere in the text. Relevant samples for analysis included only sets containing at least one implicit or explicit advice statement. Examples of coding counts and use are provided (n=213 press releases for advice analysis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal statement strength (seven-point determinism scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: For correlational research, statements of findings are rated on a seven-point scale of increasing determinism: no statement; explicit statement of no relation; correlational (e.g. 'drinking wine is associated with increased cancer rates'); ambiguous (e.g. 'drinking wine linked to cancer risk'); conditional causal (e.g. 'drinking wine might increase cancer risk'); 'can cause' (e.g. 'drinking wine can increase cancer risk'); and unconditionally causal (e.g. 'drinking wine increases cancer risk').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For press releases and news the title and first two sentences were used as the 'main statements' (inverted pyramid). For journal articles the abstract and discussion were used. The presence of stronger statements trumped weaker ones. The first claim statement was used for primary analysis; additional distinct statements were coded for replication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human inference coding for non-human studies (three levels)
rubrics_metrics.description: For studies on animals, cells, or simulations, main statements are coded as explicitly non-human, implicitly human (e.g. 'a pregnant mother’s stress level affects the brain of her unborn baby'), or explicitly human (e.g. 'a pregnant woman’s stress ...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journal article discussion and abstract were searched for any statements about human relevance. Relevant samples for analysis and counts are specified (e.g. 105 press releases, 48 with news; 115 news stories).

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveats and justifications presence
rubrics_metrics.description: Search the whole press release and news story for any caveats or justifications stated for advice, causal claims, or inference to humans (e.g. 'This is a population study. It cannot say definitively that sugary drinks raise your blood pressure...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveats and justifications were rare in press releases; their presence/absence was recorded and associations with news uptake and exaggeration were analysed. Examples and supplementary analyses referenced (SI8, SI10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Study facts and quotes coding
rubrics_metrics.description: Code factual study details and meta-information in the press release/news: sample size, study duration, completion rate, and the source of quotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These data were collected for each press release and analysed separately (see supplementary section SI11). Coding sheets for all items are available online.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main-statement selection protocol for comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Define which text spans count as the 'main statement' for comparison: for press releases and news use the title plus the first two sentences; for journal articles use the abstract and discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: most press releases/news follow the inverted pyramid and state main claims early. This protocol standardises comparisons between sources when assessing exaggeration of main claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: News uptake and coverage metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure whether a press release had any associated news story (news uptake), the number of news stories per press release, and the presence of exaggerated claims in news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses used generalized estimating equations to calculate percentages, odds ratios, and 95% confidence intervals while adjusting for clustering of several news articles to one press release. Bootstrapped confidence intervals were used for comparisons of uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion and exclusion criteria for sampled materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Include press releases based on published studies with possible relevance for human health (biomedical and psychological sciences) issued in 2011 by the Russell Group universities; include associated peer-reviewed journal articles and print/online news stories (exclude broadcast news).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sources for news included Nexis, BBC, Reuters, and Google. The sample sizes used are reported (press releases n=462; news stories n=668). The number of news stories per press release ranged from 0–10.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on correlational research for causal-claim analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Restrict causal-claim coding to correlational research designs (observational cross-sectional and longitudinal studies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualitative, interventional, or simulation designs were excluded from the causal-claims analysis. This focuses the determinism scale on situations where causal inference is particularly liable to exaggeration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of first claim statement vs multiple statements
rubrics_metrics.description: For primary analysis code the first claim statement (main claim); if a second statement occurs about a different variable pair, code it separately for replication analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach standardises which claim is compared across sources; supplementary materials (SI5) detail secondary-statement analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding reliability and quality thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure double coding and measure inter-coder reliability: in this study 27% of press releases and journal articles and 21% of news stories were double coded, with a concordance rate of 91% and mean κ = 0.88.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simulations indicated that up to 10% disagreement would not influence conclusions. Full coding instructions and all coding sheets were made publicly available to support reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive caution: using journal articles as baseline
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the peer-reviewed journal article as the baseline for detecting exaggeration but explicitly acknowledge that peer-reviewed articles are not necessarily 'true' or free of overstatement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors note that some journal articles may be over-cautious or already inflated; thus measured exaggeration (press release beyond article) may under- or over-estimate the broader issue. They recommend interpreting press-release exaggeration in light of these limitations and surveying scientist approval where possible.
